title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 811–812 (Night 170, beginning a new tale after nights-169), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 170 begins the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān, old and without an heir, prays at his vizier's urging; his wife conceives and bears a son as lovely as the full moon, whom he names Qamar al-Zamān, “Moon of the Age”. When the boy is fifteen his father, afraid for him, resolves to marry him off in his own lifetime, but Qamar al-Zamān refuses: he has read of women's guile, and quotes verses against them. The king is grieved, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلسَّبْعِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-sabʿīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing-one for the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventieth night,
sentences.n: A round number gets its own formula: al-mūfiya li-al-sabʿīn, “the one that makes up the seventy”, from awfā, Form IV, “to complete, fulfil”. li- marks the count being completed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ وَسَالِفِ الْعَصْرِ وَالْأَوَانِ مَلِكٌ يُسَمَّى الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ وَكَانَ صَاحِبَ عَسْكَرٍ عَظِيمٍ وَخَدَمٍ وَأَعْوَانٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahu kāna fī qadīmi al-zamāni wa-sālifi al-ʿaṣri wa-al-awāni malikun yusammā al-malika Shahramāna wa-kāna ṣāḥiba ʿaskarin ʿaẓīmin wa-khadamin wa-aʿwānin
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that-it (was so): there-was in the ancient-part of time and the bygone of the era and the season a king (who) is-named King Shahramān; and he-was owner of a-great army and servants and helpers.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that in olden days and ages long gone by there lived a king named King Shahramān, master of a mighty army, of servants and of retainers.
sentences.n: Here a new tale begins. annahu kāna … malikun, “that there was … a king”: the -hu is the “pronoun of the matter”, a placeholder subject, and malikun is the subject of kāna. The opening is rhymed: al-zamān / al-awān, then Shahramān / aʿwān. yusammā, passive of sammā, “to name”, takes the name as a second object, hence accusative al-malika Shahramāna (a diptote, so no tanwīn). ṣāḥib, “owner, possessor”, governs all three genitives: ʿaskar, “army”, khadam, “servants” (a collective), and aʿwān, “helpers”.

sentences.t: إِلَّا أَنَّهُ كَانَ قَدْ كَبِرَ سِنُّهُ وَرَقَّ عَظْمُهُ وَلَمْ يُرْزَقْ بِوَلَدٍ
sentences.tr: illā annahu kāna qad kabira sinnuhu wa-raqqa ʿaẓmuhu wa-lam yurzaq bi-waladin
sentences.l: Except that-he had already grown-great his-age, and thin-become his-bone, and he-was-not-granted a-child.
sentences.i: Yet he had grown old in years, his bones had worn thin, and he had not been blessed with a son.
sentences.n: illā anna, “except that”, i.e. “but, however”. kāna qad + perfect gives the pluperfect: “had grown”. kabira sinnuhu, “his age became great”; raqqa ʿaẓmuhu, “his bone grew thin”, a stock phrase for frailty in old age. yurzaq, passive of razaqa, “to provide (as God provides)”: “he was not granted”; bi- marks the gift. walad is “child”, but in such contexts it means a son and heir.

sentences.t: فَتَفَكَّرَ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَحَزِنَ وَقَلِقَ وَشَكَى ذَلِكَ لِبَعْضِ وُزَرَائِهِ وَقَالَ إِنِّي أَخَافُ إِذَا مُتُّ ضَاعَ الْمُلْكُ لِأَنِّي لَمْ أَجِدْ مَنْ يَتَوَلَّاهُ بَعْدِي مِنْ وَلَدِي
sentences.tr: fa-tafakkara fī nafsihi wa-ḥazina wa-qaliqa wa-shakā dhālika li-baʿḍi wuzarāʾihi wa-qāla innī akhāfu idhā muttu ḍāʿa al-mulku li-annī lam ajid man yatawallāhu baʿdī min waladī
sentences.l: And he-pondered in himself, and grieved, and was-troubled, and complained-of that to some-of his-viziers, and said: Truly-I fear (that) if I-die the kingship is-lost, because-I have-not found one-who will-take-it-in-charge after-me from my-offspring.
sentences.i: He brooded over it inwardly, grieving and uneasy, and he laid his trouble before one of his viziers. “I fear,” he said, “that when I die the kingdom will be lost, for I have found no child of mine to take it up after me.”
sentences.n: tafakkara, Form V, “to ponder”; fī nafsihi, “within himself”. شكى is the print's spelling of shakā, which Classical Arabic writes شكا with alif; the edition often writes such verbs with ى. li-baʿḍi wuzarāʾihi, “to one of his viziers”: baʿḍ, “some, a certain one of”, and li- marks the one complained to; the next sentence shows it was a single vizier. akhāfu idhā muttu ḍāʿa al-mulku: the fear is stated without “that”, a looser, conversational construction. al-mulk, “kingship, rule”, not al-malik, “king”. yatawallāhu, Form V, “to take charge of it”. min waladī, “from my offspring”: walad here collective.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ ذَلِكَ الْوَزِيرُ لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَمْرًا فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ وَابْتَهِلْ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu dhālika al-wazīru laʿalla Allāha yuḥdithu baʿda dhālika amran fa-tawakkal ʿalā Allāhi ayyuhā al-maliku wa-ibtahil ilayhi
sentences.l: And that vizier said to-him: Perhaps God will-bring-about after that a-matter; so rely on God, O king, and supplicate to-Him.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “It may be that God will bring something new to pass hereafter. Put your trust in God, O king, and humble yourself before Him in prayer.”
sentences.n: laʿalla, “perhaps”, behaves like inna: its subject Allāha is accusative. laʿalla Allāha yuḥdithu baʿda dhālika amran echoes the Qurʾān (65:1), “perhaps God will bring about after that some new thing”. tawakkal, Form V imperative, “rely”, takes ʿalā for the one relied on. ibtahala, Form VIII, “to pray humbly, supplicate”, with ilā for the one addressed.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ الْمَلِكُ وَتَوَضَّأَ وَصَلَّى رَكْعَتَيْنِ وَدَعَى اللَّهَ تَعَالَى بِنِيَّةٍ صَادِقَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma al-maliku wa-tawaḍḍaʾa wa-ṣallā rakʿatayni wa-daʿā Allāha taʿālā bi-niyyatin ṣādiqatin
sentences.l: And the king arose, and made-ablution, and prayed two-bowings, and called-upon God (exalted is He) with a-sincere intention.
sentences.i: So the king rose, made his ablutions, prayed two cycles of prayer, and called upon God Most High with a sincere heart.
sentences.n: tawaḍḍaʾa, Form V, “to perform the wuḍūʾ”, the washing before prayer; its hamza is printed. rakʿatayn, dual of rakʿa, one cycle of bowing and prostration: a short voluntary prayer. دعى is daʿā spelled with ى, as شكى above; the next sentence prints the same verb دعا with alif. bi-niyyatin ṣādiqatin, “with a true intention”: bi- of manner.

sentences.t: وَدَعَا زَوْجَتَهُ لِلْفِرَاشِ وَجَامَعَهَا فِي ذَلِكَ الْوَقْتِ فَعَلِقَتْ مِنْهُ بِقُدْرَةِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: wa-daʿā zawjatahu li-al-firāshi wa-jāmaʿahā fī dhālika al-waqti fa-ʿaliqat minhu bi-qudrati Allāhi taʿālā
sentences.l: And he-called his-wife to the bed, and lay-with-her in that time; and she-conceived from-him by the power of God (exalted is He).
sentences.i: Then he called his wife to bed and lay with her that very hour, and by the power of God Most High she conceived by him.
sentences.n: The same verb daʿā, now in its everyday sense “to call, summon”, with li- for where she is called to. jāmaʿa, Form III, “to have intercourse with”. ʿaliqat minhu, “she conceived from him”, the usual verb for conception. bi-qudrati Allāh, “by God's power”: bi- of means.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَمَلَتْ أَشْهُرُهَا وَضَعَتْ وَلَدًا ذَكَرًا كَأَنَّهُ الْبَدْرُ لَيْلَةَ تَمَامِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kamalat ashhuruhā waḍaʿat waladan dhakaran ka-annahu al-badru laylata tamāmihi
sentences.l: And when her-months were-complete, she-bore a-male child, as-though-he (were) the full-moon (on the) night of its-completion.
sentences.i: When her months were fulfilled she gave birth to a boy, like the moon on the night it rounds to full.
sentences.n: ashhur, a plural of shahr, “month”, used for small numbers: “her months” of pregnancy. waḍaʿat, “she laid down”, the usual verb for giving birth. walad dhakar, “a male child”. ka-anna, “as though”: ka-, “like”, + anna. al-badr is the full moon; laylata tamāmihi, “on the night of its completion”, accusative of time.

sentences.t: فَسَمَّاهُ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ وَفَرِحَ بِهِ غَايَةَ الْفَرَحِ
sentences.tr: fa-sammāhu Qamara al-Zamāni wa-fariḥa bihi ghāyata al-faraḥi
sentences.l: And he-named-him Qamar al-Zamān, and rejoiced in-him the utmost of joy.
sentences.i: He named him Qamar al-Zamān, and his joy in him knew no bounds.
sentences.n: Qamar al-Zamān means “Moon of the Age”, a name that picks up the full-moon image just before it; he gives this tale its name. sammā takes two objects: the child (-hu) and the name (Qamara al-Zamāni, accusative). fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice in”: the verb chooses bi- for the cause of joy. ghāyata al-faraḥ, “the utmost of joy”, an accusative that intensifies the verb.

sentences.t: وَنَادَى بِالزِّيّنَةِ فَزُيِّنَتِ الْمَدِينَةُ سَبْعَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَدُقَّتِ الطُّبُولُ وَأَقْبَلَتِ الْبَشَائِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-nādā bi-al-zīnati fa-zuyyinati al-madīnatu sabʿata ayyāmin wa-duqqati al-ṭubūlu wa-aqbalati al-bashāʾiru
sentences.l: And he-proclaimed the adornment, and the city was-adorned seven days, and the drums were-beaten, and the glad-tidings came-forward.
sentences.i: He had the decking of the city proclaimed, and for seven days it was hung with finery; the drums were beaten, and the bearers of good news came flocking in.
sentences.n: nādā bi-, “to proclaim, have cried abroad”: bi- marks what is proclaimed. al-zīna, “adornment”, the public decorating of a city for a royal celebration. The print sets the shadda of بالزيّنة over the yāʾ, where it fits no reading; it is kept where the print has it, and the word is read al-zīna (the article's l assimilated to the z). zuyyinat, passive of zayyana, “to adorn”, and duqqat, passive of daqqa, “to beat”. al-bashāʾir, “good tidings”, here the messengers or gifts that bring them; the hamza is printed.

sentences.t: وَرُتِّبَتْ لَهُ الْمَرَاضِعُ وَالدَّايَاتُ وَتَرَبَّى فِى الْعِزِّ وَالدَّلَالِ حَتَّى صَارَ لَهُ مِنَ الْعُمْرِ خَمْسَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً
sentences.tr: wa-ruttibat lahu al-marāḍiʿu wa-al-dāyātu wa-tarabbā fī al-ʿizzi wa-al-dalāli ḥattā ṣāra lahu mina al-ʿumri khamsa ʿashrata sanatan
sentences.l: And there-were-appointed for-him the wet-nurses and the nursemaids, and he-was-brought-up in honour and indulgence until there-became to-him of age fifteen years.
sentences.i: Wet-nurses and nursemaids were appointed for him, and he was reared in honour and tender indulgence until he reached the age of fifteen.
sentences.n: ruttibat, passive of rattaba, “to arrange, assign”. marāḍiʿ, plural of murḍiʿ, “wet-nurse”; dāyāt, plural of dāya, “nurse, midwife”. tarabbā, Form V, “to be brought up”. فى is the print's spelling of fī. ṣāra lahu mina al-ʿumri …, “there came to be to him, of age, …”: li- marks the one whose age it is, the usual way to say “he reached the age of”. khamsa ʿashrata, “fifteen”, in the feminine form because sana, “year”, is feminine; the counted noun after eleven to ninety-nine is accusative singular.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فَائِقًا فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ وَالْقَدِّ وَالِاعْتِدَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fāʾiqan fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli wa-al-qaddi wa-al-iʿtidāli
sentences.l: And he-was surpassing in comeliness and beauty and stature and straightness.
sentences.i: He surpassed all others in grace and beauty, in stature and in fine proportion.
sentences.n: fāʾiq, “excelling”, active participle of fāqa; its hamza is printed. Two rhymed pairs: ḥusn and jamāl, both “beauty”; qadd, “figure, stature”, and iʿtidāl, Form VIII verbal noun, “evenness, good proportion”, of a straight upright body.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ أَبُوهُ يُحِبُّهُ وَلَا يَقْدِرُ أَنْ يُفَارِقَهُ لَيْلًا وَلَا نَهَارًا
sentences.tr: wa-kāna abūhu yuḥibbuhu wa-lā yaqdiru an yufāriqahu laylan wa-lā nahāran
sentences.l: And his-father loved-him and could not part-from-him by-night nor by-day.
sentences.i: His father loved him dearly and could not bear to be parted from him by night or by day.
sentences.n: kāna + imperfect describes an ongoing state in the past: “he used to love him”. abūhu, nominative of ab, “father”, with the long ū before a suffix. yaqdiru an, “he is able to”, with the subjunctive yufāriqa. laylan wa-lā nahāran, accusatives of time.

sentences.t: فَشَكَى أَبُوهُ لِبَعْضِ وُزَرَائِهِ زِيَادَةَ حُبِّهِ لَهُ وَقَالَ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ إِنِّي خَائِفٌ عَلَى وَلَدِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ طَوَارِقِ الدَّهْرِ وَالْحَدَثَانِ وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ أُزَوِّجَهُ فِي حَيٰوتِي
sentences.tr: fa-shakā abūhu li-baʿḍi wuzarāʾihi ziyādata ḥubbihi lahu wa-qāla ayyuhā al-wazīru innī khāʾifun ʿalā waladī Qamari al-Zamāni min ṭawāriqi al-dahri wa-al-ḥadathāni wa-urīdu an uzawwijahu fī ḥayātī
sentences.l: And his-father complained to one-of his-viziers (of) the excess of his-love for-him, and said: O vizier, I (am) fearful for my-son Qamar al-Zamān of the night-comers of time and the happenings, and I-want that I-marry-him-off in my-life.
sentences.i: Then his father opened his heart to one of his viziers, telling him how beyond all measure he loved the boy, and said, “Vizier, I fear for my son Qamar al-Zamān from the blows that time and its chances bring by night, and I wish to see him married while I still live.”
sentences.n: shakā li-, “to complain to”: Classical says shakā ilā; li- for ilā is a Middle Arabic habit. The thing complained of, ziyādata ḥubbihi, is the direct object: the father's grievance is the excess of his own love. ṭawāriq, plural of ṭāriqa, “what comes knocking by night”, hence sudden calamities; al-ḥadathān, “the happenings” of night and day, the chances of fortune. The rhyme Zamān / ḥadathān is sajʿ. uzawwijahu, Form II, “to give (someone) in marriage”; the shadda is printed. حيٰوتي is ḥayātī, “my life”, in the old spelling of ḥayāh with w and the dagger alif (printed): fī ḥayātī, “in my lifetime”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ أَنَّ الزَّوَاجَ مِنْ مَكَارِمِ الْأَخْلَاقِ وَالصَّوَابُ أَنْ تُزَوِّجَ وَلَدَكَ فِي حَيٰوتِكَ قَبْلَ أَنْ تُسَلْطِنَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru iʿlam ayyuhā al-maliku anna al-zawāja min makārimi al-akhlāqi wa-al-ṣawābu an tuzawwija waladaka fī ḥayātika qabla an tusalṭinahu
sentences.l: And the vizier said to-him: Know, O king, that the marrying (is) of the noble-points of the characters, and the right-course (is) that you-marry-off your-son in your-life before that you-make-him-sultan.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “Know, O king, that marriage is among the noblest of virtues, and the right course is for you to marry your son in your own lifetime, before you make him sultan.”
sentences.n: min makārimi al-akhlāqi, “among the noble traits of character”: makārim, plural of makrama, “a noble deed or quality”. al-ṣawābu an …, “the right thing is that …”. tusalṭinahu, from the four-letter verb salṭana, “to make (someone) sultan”, a later coinage from sulṭān; the vizier advises marrying the prince off before handing him the throne.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَالَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ عَلَيَّ بِوَلَدِي قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāla al-maliku Shahramānu ʿalayya bi-waladī Qamari al-Zamāni
sentences.l: And at that, King Shahramān said: Upon-me with my-son Qamar al-Zamān!
sentences.i: At that King Shahramān said, “Bring me my son Qamar al-Zamān.”
sentences.n: ʿalayya bi-, literally “upon me with”, is a set command: “bring me …”; bi- marks what is to be fetched. The shadda of عليّ is printed. Qamari al-Zamāni stands in apposition to waladī and so is genitive. Shahramān, a foreign name in -ān, is diptote: nominative -u, no nunation.

sentences.t: فَحَضَرَ وَأَطْرَقَ بِرَأْسِهِ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ حَيَاءً مِنْ أَبِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥaḍara wa-aṭraqa bi-raʾsihi ilā al-arḍi ḥayāʾan min abīhi
sentences.l: And he-came-present and lowered with his-head to the ground, out-of-modesty from his-father.
sentences.i: He came, and bowed his head to the ground in bashfulness before his father.
sentences.n: aṭraqa, Form IV, “to bow the head, look down in silence”; with bi-raʾsihi, “with his head”, bi- marks the part of the body that is lowered. ḥayāʾan, accusative of reason: “out of modesty”. The hamza of برأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَبُوهُ يَا قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُزَوِّجَكَ وَأَفْرَحَ بِكَ فِى حَيٰوتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu abūhu yā Qamara al-Zamāni innī urīdu an uzawwijaka wa-afraḥa bika fī ḥayātī
sentences.l: And his-father said to-him: O Qamar al-Zamān, I want that I-marry-you-off and rejoice in-you in my-life.
sentences.i: His father said to him, “Qamar al-Zamān, I wish to see you married and have joy of you while I live.”
sentences.n: yā Qamara al-Zamāni: a name made of two words in construct takes the accusative after yā. afraḥa is still governed by an, so subjunctive; fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice in, have joy of”: the verb chooses bi-. فى is the print's spelling of fī, with ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا أَبِي اعْلَمْ أَنَّ مَالِي فِى الزَّوَاجِ رَغْبَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā abī iʿlam anna mā lī fī al-zawāji raghbatun
sentences.l: And he-said to-him: O my-father, know that not to-me in the marrying (is) a-desire.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Father, know that I have no wish to marry.”
sentences.n: مالي is mā lī, “I have not”, the negative mā and lī, “to me”, set as one word as the print often does; it is not mālī, “my wealth”. Classical grammar would want a pronoun after anna (annahu mā lī …); the text runs anna straight on into a negative clause, a common Middle Arabic looseness. raghbatun, “desire”, is the subject of the nominal clause, so nominative.

sentences.t: وَنَفْسِي لَا تَمِيلُ إِلَى النِّسَاءِ لِأَنِّي وَجَدْتُ فِي مَكْرِهِنَّ وَغَدْرِهِنَّ كُتُبًا وَكَلَامًا كَثِيرًا كَمَا قَالَ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-nafsī lā tamīlu ilā al-nisāʾi li-annī wajadtu fī makrihinna wa-ghadrihinna kutuban wa-kalāman kathīran kamā qāla al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And my-soul does not incline to the women, because I found on their-(f.)-guile and their-treachery books and talk much, as the poet said:
sentences.i: “My soul has no leaning towards women, for I have found books and a great deal of talk on their cunning and their treachery, as the poet says:
sentences.n: nafs, “soul, self”, is feminine, hence tamīlu. li-annī, “because I”. fī here is “on, about”: books written on the subject. -hinna, “their”, feminine plural. The verses that follow are Qamar al-Zamān's own quotation.

sentences.t:
فَاِنْ تَسْأَلُوْنِي بِالنِّسَاءِ فَاِنَّنِيْ * خَبِيْرٌ بِاَحْوَالِ النِّسَاءِ طَبِيْبُ
اِذَا شَابَ رَأْسُ الْمَرْءِ اَوْقَلَّ مَالُهُ * فَلَيْسَ لَهُ مِنْ وُدِّهِنَّ نَصِيْبُ
sentences.tr:
fa-in tasʾalūnī bi-al-nisāʾi fa-innanī * khabīrun bi-aḥwāli al-nisāʾi ṭabību
idhā shāba raʾsu al-marʾi aw qalla māluhu * fa-laysa lahu min wuddihinna naṣību
sentences.l:
And if you-ask-me about the women, then I (am) * expert in the conditions of the women, a-physician.
When the head of the man turns-white or his-wealth grows-little, * then there-is-not for-him of their-(f.)-love a-share.
sentences.i:
If it is women you ask me about, I know them well, a physician versed in all their moods:
once a man's head turns grey or his money runs short, he has no share left in their love.
sentences.n: Lines from an ode of the pre-Islamic poet ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada. saʾala bi-, “to ask about”: bi- marks the subject of the question; in bi-aḥwāli, “in the conditions”, bi- goes with khabīr, “expert in”. ṭabībun is a second predicate: “an expert, a physician”. The print sets aw qalla, “or (it) grows little”, run together as اَوْقَلَّ, the sukūn of aw sitting on the w; read it as two words. The sukūn the print puts on long vowels (تَسْأَلُوْنِي, خَبِيْرٌ) is its habit in verse and marks nothing more. The rhyme is -ību, with the u lengthened at the line's end.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْآخَرُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-ākharu
sentences.l: And the other said:
sentences.i: And another said:
sentences.n: al-ākhar, “the other”, here another poet. The madda of الآخر is the print's own.

sentences.t:
اِعْصِ النِّسَاءَ فَتِلْكَ الطَّاعَةُ الْحَسَنَهْ * فَلَنْ يَفُوْزَ فَتًى يُعْطِى النِّسَا رَسَنَهْ
يَعُقْنَهُ عَنْ كَمَالٍ فِي فَضَائِلِهِ * وَلَوْ سَعَى طَالِبًا لِلْعِلْمِ اَلْفَ سَنَهْ
sentences.tr:
iʿṣi al-nisāʾa fa-tilka al-ṭāʿatu al-ḥasanah * fa-lan yafūza fatan yuʿṭī al-nisā rasanah
yaʿuqnahu ʿan kamālin fī faḍāʾilihi * wa-law saʿā ṭāliban li-al-ʿilmi alfa sanah
sentences.l:
Disobey the women, for that (is) the obedience, the good-one; * for never will-win a-youth (who) gives the women his-halter.
They-(f.)-hinder-him from perfection in his-merits, * even-if he-strove, seeking for the knowledge, a-thousand years.
sentences.i:
Disobey women: that is obedience rightly done. No young man will ever prosper who puts his halter in women's hands.
They will keep him from reaching the full measure of his gifts, though he toil a thousand years in the pursuit of learning.
sentences.n: iʿṣi, imperative of ʿaṣā, yaʿṣī, “to disobey”: the long ī of the stem is shortened to i, as in the jussive. The rhyme is -anah, and the print spells it with هْ throughout, though the h is two different things: in al-ḥasanah and sanah it is the feminine ending (ة) read in pause, in rasanah it is the pronoun, rasana-hu, “his halter”. To hand someone your halter (rasan, a rope or bridle) is to let them lead you. al-nisā is nisāʾ shortened for the metre. The print writes يُعْطِى with ى, as it does فى; the word is yuʿṭī, “gives”, active, and should not be read yuʿṭā. yaʿuqnahu, from ʿāqa, yaʿūqu, “to hinder”: feminine plural, “they (women) hinder him”. li-al-ʿilmi, “for knowledge”: li- marks what he seeks.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ قَالَ يَا أَبِي إِنَّ الزَّوَاجَ شَيْءٌ لَا أَفْعَلُهُ أَبَدًا وَلَوْ سُقِيتُ كَأْسَ الرَّدَى
sentences.tr: wa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi qāla yā abī inna al-zawāja shayʾun lā afʿaluhu abadan wa-law suqītu kaʾsa al-radā
sentences.l: And when he-finished from his-verse, he-said: O my-father, the marrying (is) a-thing I do not do-it ever, even-if I-were-given-to-drink the cup of the perdition.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he said, “Father, marriage is a thing I will never do, not though I were made to drink the cup of death.”
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”. lā afʿaluhu abadan, “I will never do it”: the imperfect with lā and abadan looks to the future. suqītu, passive of saqā, “to give to drink”; the ḍamma of سقيتُ is printed, and marks the first person. al-radā, “ruin, death”. The hamzas of شيء and كأس are printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ السُّلْطَانُ شَهْرَمَانُ مِنْ وَلَدِهِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ صَارَ الضِّيَاءُ فِي وَجْهِهِ ظَلَامًا وَاغْتَمَّ لِذَلِكَ غَمًّا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-sulṭānu Shahramānu min waladihi hādhā al-kalāma ṣāra al-ḍiyāʾu fī wajhihi ẓalāman wa-ightamma li-dhālika ghamman shadīdan
sentences.l: And when the Sultan Shahramān heard from his-son this speech, the light in his-face became darkness, and he-grieved for that a-grieving severe.
sentences.i: When Sultan Shahramān heard these words from his son, the light in his face turned to darkness, and he was sorely grieved at it.
sentences.n: The king is now called sulṭān; the text uses the two titles interchangeably. ṣāra … ẓalāman, “became darkness”: ṣāra takes its predicate in the accusative. ightamma, Form VIII, “to be grieved”, with li-, “at, on account of”; ghamman shadīdan, its own verbal noun used to intensify, “with a heavy grief”. The shadda of غمّا is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد; the spacing is kept. The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning.
